summary: The Solar Impulse, an experimental solar-powered airplane, landed in Switzerland after completing a 26-hour test flight that demonstrated a solar-powered aircraft can accumulate enough daytime energy to power it through the night, and the team says the plane could fly indefinitely in theory given sufficient sunlight. The flight — the longest and highest by a piloted solar-powered aircraft — averaged about 28,000 feet and 25 miles per hour, and pilot Andre Borschberg, a former Swiss air force fighter pilot, said he had flown more than 26 hours without using fuel or causing pollution. The single-passenger plane contains 12,000 solar cells but faced setbacks such as a sore back, a ten-hour period at minus twenty degrees Celsius in the cockpit that froze the drinking water system and drained iPod batteries; the project aims to show emissions-free air travel is feasible though the team does not expect current propulsion methods to be replaced in the near future.
